paraphrase: When the group-of-six monks learned and taught low arts (tiracchāna-vijjā), the Buddha laid down: monks, low arts are not to be learned — whoever learns them commits an offence of wrong-doing; nor are they to be taught.
notes: For nuns learning low arts is a pācittiya offence (Bhikkhunī Pācittiya 49). Phase-B spot check: wording/locator matched against a local e-text in sources_raw/ (GRETIL / eBhāratī / bilara-data); not a formal Phase-C sourcing check.

paraphrase: A Rājagaha merchant hung a sandalwood bowl on a bamboo pole for 'any ascetic or brahmin who is an arahant with powers'. Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita, Pakudha, Sañjaya and the Nigaṇṭha each came claiming 'I am an arahant with powers — give me the bowl', and were told to take it down; Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja rose into the air and took it. The Buddha rebuked him and forbade monks to display superhuman powers to lay people.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Vinaya Cullavagga (Buddhist Pali canon). SuttaCentral pli-tv-kd15:8. The rebuke is recalled from the same section; the local check confirmed the six teachers' claims.

paraphrase: Sañjaya the wanderer lived at Rājagaha with 250 wanderers, among them Sāriputta and Moggallāna. After Sāriputta heard the verse on causes from Assaji, the two went to the Buddha with the 250; Sañjaya refused to come, and hot blood gushed from his mouth.
notes: Reported by an opponent: the Vinaya Mahāvagga (Buddhist Pali canon). SuttaCentral pli-tv-kd1:23–24. The Vinaya calls him only 'Sañjaya the wanderer'.
